# Measuring what written context is worth

This skill drives the `contextlift` command. It does not replace it.

**Every guard lives in the command, not here.** The budget, the count of holdout
reads, the forbidden-project list, and the two typed confirmations are enforced
inside the CLI, and `ask_tty` reads them from `/dev/tty` rather than from stdin.
So a host agent cannot approve a paid run or a second holdout read on the user's
behalf, whatever it is asked to do. That is deliberate. Do not try to work around
it; report the refusal and let the person type.

## Say the cost before any paid step

Every command that spends money prints a cost sheet first. Show it to the person
and wait. Do not pass `--yes` unless they asked for it in this conversation, and
never pass `--force`.

Free: `contextlift demo`, `contextlift split`, `contextlift arms`, `contextlift classes`,
`contextlift leak`, `contextlift build-examples`, `contextlift worklist`, `contextlift share`,
`contextlift next`, `contextlift eval-room`, `contextlift spec-push --dry-run`.

Cents: `contextlift gate` (it runs every gold once), `contextlift spec-push`,
`contextlift catalog-rollback`, `contextlift sentinel`.

Dollars: `contextlift round`, `contextlift generate`, `contextlift review --draft`, and
`contextlift mine` when it drafts questions.

## The one thing that goes wrong most

**A number that looks good and means nothing.** The three ways it happens, and what
the tool does about each:

- The answer key is wrong. `gate` audits it first, with 12 defect classes. A
  benchmark's own published golds failed it at 52.8% once. Run `gate` before
  believing any score.
- The lift was measured on the questions the context was written from. `split`
  seals a reserved set and the verdict prints OVERFIT when the working set moved
  and the reserved one did not.
- The set is too small to show anything. The verdict says UNDERPOWERED and prints
  how many questions would be needed. **UNDERPOWERED is not a failure and not a
  bug. Do not suggest re-running it to get a different word.**

## A count is not a cause. Read the pairs.

The lever prints something like "16 of 28 failures are COLUMN_COUNT: worked
examples". That is a **count**. It is not a diagnosis, and its own last line
says so: "Read three failing pairs side by side before writing anything."

Do that. On 2026-09-10 it changed the answer completely. The count said write
16 worked examples. The pairs showed one shared cause behind 13 of them:

    question: "return rate by department"
    gold:     department, return_pct
    model:    department, returned, non_cancelled, return_pct

Every rate question returned the answer AND the numerator and denominator it
came from. One convention, one written rule line - not sixteen examples.

So before writing anything, read the failing pairs and ask: **is there one
cause behind many of these?** A host agent handed "write 16 examples" will
write 16 examples, and sixteen items nobody needed are sixteen things to
maintain and sixteen chances to leak a scored question.

Two more things the pairs tell you that the count cannot:

- **Whether the answer key is at fault.** A gold returning columns the
  question never names is under-specified, and a worked example papers over
  it. `gate` already warns about this as MISSING_PROJECTION. Fix the gold
  instead.
- **Whether a metric is already declared somewhere.** If the estate has
  LookML, dbt, Cube or an Apache Ossie file, the convention may be written
  down already. `contextlift semantic` reads it, and a declared metric beats a
  rule somebody has to remember to write.

## Start here

    contextlift demo

No key, no cloud, 0.14 seconds. Show a person what a round looks like before
asking them for credentials.

## The loop

    contextlift next --workspace .

`next` reads the workspace and prints the one command to run now, with why. Prefer
it over choosing a command yourself: it knows which stage the person is at and
what the last run said.

The stages, in order:

1. `contextlift mine` or write questions, then `contextlift review` them into a gold set
2. `contextlift gate --db ... --golds golds.csv` — audit the answer key. Read the flagged rows.
3. `contextlift split --golds golds.csv` — seal the reserved set
4. `contextlift round --golds ... --spec ... --db ...` — two arms, one verdict
5. `contextlift worklist --run RUN.csv --spec DIR` — which context item to look at first
6. `contextlift classes --spec DIR --golds ...` — what a whole class of context is worth
7. `contextlift build-examples` if the lever says worked examples
8. write context, `git commit`, go back to 4

## Reading a verdict

The word comes first and the order matters: INVALID, then REAL GAIN or REAL LOSS,
then OVERFIT, then UNDERPOWERED, then NO CHANGE, then NOT PROVEN.

Always read three lines together, not the lift alone:

- **the gap**, working-set lift minus reserved lift. If its interval excludes zero
  the context fitted the questions it was written from.
- **how many questions the number rests on**, which is not how many were asked. A
  round once printed "23 questions" for a number resting on one.
- **lookups**. If answers "ran a stored example instead of writing SQL" they are
  excluded, and a large count means the arm was not measured as a text-to-SQL
  system at all.

## Never do these

- Do not read the reserved set to decide what to write next. That is what turns it
  into training data. The working set is for that.
- Do not pass `--force` to get a second holdout read.
- Do not quote a working-set lift as the result. It is labelled "fit on the working
  questions" for a reason.
- Do not put customer question text, SQL, or table names into a chat message, a
  ticket or a commit. `contextlift share` is the only way out of an estate: it sends
  counts, lengths, pass-or-fail and pseudonyms, and refuses the whole export if a
  real name survives into it.

## What the person should know before they start

A second model sees the workspace when this skill runs, and the workspace holds
their questions and their SQL. Say so.

## The one bypass, and why it is not blocked here

`--yes` skips the typed confirmation. It is the only way to spend money
without a person typing, and it is the user's to ask for, never yours to add.

It cannot be used alone: the command refuses `--yes` without `--budget`, with
"a yes with no ceiling is a blank cheque". So an approved run still has a hard
ceiling on it.

This extension does not put `--yes` in `excludeTools`. That list matches a
tool call by prefix, so a block on `contextlift round --yes` is defeated by
moving the flag further along the line. A guard that looks enforced and is not
is worse than a rule written down.
